testCases.name: test_case_0
testCases.input: What is the difference between model evals and application evals?
testCases.actualOutput:
To understand the difference between these two concepts, it helps to think about what exactly you are trying to measure. In this course, we categorize evaluations into two types: model evals and application evals.

Model evals are designed to evaluate the LLM itself. The primary goal here is to test and document the inherent capabilities of a model—such as its proficiency in math, reasoning, or instruction following—often when a new model is released. These are typically conducted using standardized tests known as benchmarks, which provide a way to compare models on leaderboards. However, you can also run custom model evals by creating your own dataset if you need to see how a specific model performs for your particular needs.

On the other hand, application evals are used to evaluate LLM-based applications. While model evals look at the "raw" capabilities of the model, application evals focus on how well the entire system performs in the context of its specific use case. For example, if you built a system to automatically route customer emails into categories like billing or technical support, an application eval would test how effectively that specific system handles those tasks.

It is important to note that "model eval" and "application eval" are not official industry terms; they are simplified labels used in this course to help clarify the distinction between evaluating the underlying model versus evaluating the end-to-end application. In the industry, both are generally referred to as "LLM evals," and the specific type is usually understood based on the context of the use case.

testCases.name: test_case_1
testCases.input: What is the difference between reference-based and reference-free evaluation?
testCases.actualOutput:
To understand the difference between these two types of evaluation, it helps to think about whether or not you have an "answer key" to check your work against.

In a **reference-based evaluation**, you have a "golden dataset" that contains a known, correct answer for every test case. When you grade the model's output, you are essentially comparing what the model generated against this pre-defined reference answer to see how well it matches. A common example of this would be something like a UPSC exam, where there is a specific, correct answer that you can use to grade the response.

On the other hand, a **reference-free evaluation** is used when you do not have a golden dataset or a pre-defined answer key. In this scenario, you cannot simply compare the output to a "correct" version. Instead, you rely on other methods, such as using a rubric or human judgment, to decide if the model's response is correct or to assign it a score (for example, on a scale of 1 to 5). Because there is no objective "correct answer" provided in the data, you are evaluating the quality of the response based on the criteria defined in your rubric.

In short, the simplest way to classify an evaluation pipeline is to ask yourself: "Is the correct answer provided in my golden dataset?" If the answer is yes, it is reference-based; if it is not, it is reference-free.

testCases.name: test_case_2
testCases.input: What is the difference between offline evals and online evals?
testCases.actualOutput:
To understand the difference between offline and online evaluations, it is helpful to think of them as complementary tools rather than rivals; you need both to ensure your application is successful.

The primary distinction lies in when they occur and what they measure. Offline evaluation happens before you deploy your software. Its main purpose is to check if your application is working correctly. Because you are running this on a fixed, curated set of data—often called a "golden data set"—it is fast, cheap, and repeatable. You can use the results of these evaluations for "gating," which means if your performance score meets a certain threshold, you can automatically push your code to production using CI (Continuous Integration).

Online evaluation, on the other hand, takes place after your software is deployed and is running on live production traffic. Its purpose is to tell you if your application is running normally in the real world. A key characteristic of online evaluation is that it works without a golden data set or an answer key, which is critical because you cannot predict what questions real users will ask once the system is live. Because monitoring every single interaction—such as 50,000 daily conversations—can be costly, online evaluation often utilizes a "sampling" technique where you randomly monitor a smaller subset of those conversations to manage costs.

In summary, while offline evaluation acts as a gatekeeper to verify correctness before launch, online evaluation provides ongoing monitoring for drift detection and ensures your system continues to perform properly as it encounters unpredictable, real-world usage.

testCases.name: test_case_3
testCases.input: Why do we need custom model evals if public benchmarks already exist?
testCases.actualOutput:
It is a great question to ask why we would need custom evaluations when standardized benchmarks are already available. To understand this, it helps to think of benchmarks as standardized tests—like a general aptitude exam—that measure broad, generic capabilities such as reasoning, mathematics, or coding proficiency. While these benchmarks are useful for understanding how a model performs in a general sense, they often don't tell the whole story when it comes to your specific needs.

The primary reason we need custom evaluations is that benchmarks may not reflect how a model will perform on your unique application and data. A model might score exceptionally well on a public benchmark, but that doesn't guarantee it is the most suitable or cost-effective choice for your specific use case. 

For example, you might be choosing between two models where "Model A" consistently outperforms "Model B" on every public benchmark. However, if you run a custom evaluation using your own data, you might discover that "Model B" is actually the better choice. It might provide sufficient accuracy for your specific task while offering significant savings in terms of cost and latency. If you had relied solely on public benchmarks, you would have missed that better value proposition. 

In short, while benchmarks help you understand the generic capabilities of a model, custom evaluations allow you to test a model against your own data and scoring mechanisms. This ensures that you are selecting the model that is truly the best fit for your specific application, especially when dealing with niche domains like financial services or law where general benchmarks might not capture the nuances of your work.

testCases.name: test_case_4
testCases.input: What are the component, pipeline and application levels of evaluation in a RAG system?
testCases.actualOutput:
When evaluating a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) chatbot, we use a multi-layered approach because a single evaluation pipeline cannot capture every potential point of failure. To ensure a robust system, we test at three distinct levels:

At the **component level**, we evaluate the individual building blocks of your application. For a RAG system, this means testing the retriever and the generator separately. For example, when evaluating the retriever, you would assess its performance based on specific criteria like retrieval accuracy to ensure it is fetching the correct information.

At the **pipeline level**, we evaluate how these components work together once they are connected. The standard framework used here is the "RAG triad," which examines the relationship between three key elements: the user's question, the context retrieved from your vector database, and the answer generated by the model. Within this triad, we measure three specific metrics: context relevance (is the retrieved context actually useful for the user's question?), faithfulness (is the generated answer derived strictly from the provided context?), and answer relevance (does the answer directly address the user's question?).

Finally, at the **application or system level**, we evaluate the chatbot as a whole to ensure it meets broader quality standards. At this stage, we focus on metrics such as correctness and completeness to verify that the system is providing accurate and comprehensive responses to the end user. 

By testing across these three levels—component, pipeline, and application—you create a comprehensive evaluation suite that allows you to identify failures at every stage of the RAG process before deployment.

testCases.actualOutput:
To explain the evaluation of RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) applications, we look at the process through a structured framework that ensures each part of the system is performing correctly.

The first level is **component-level evaluation**. In this stage, we test the individual building blocks of the RAG system separately. This involves building a retriever and testing its performance, followed by building a generator and testing its specific output. By isolating these components, we can ensure that each part is functioning as intended before they are integrated.

The second level is the **RAG pipeline evaluation**, which occurs once the retriever and generator are connected. At this stage, we use a framework known as the "RAG triad." This triad evaluates the relationship between three key elements: the user's question, the context retrieved from the vector database, and the answer generated by the model. Within this triad, we measure three specific metrics:
*   **Context Relevance:** This checks if the context fetched by the retriever is actually relevant to the user's question.
*   **Faithfulness:** This evaluates the relationship between the generated answer and the retrieved context to ensure the answer is grounded in the provided information.
*   **Answer Relevance:** This assesses how well the final answer addresses the user's original question.

The third level involves **application-level evaluation**. This is a broader assessment where we evaluate the entire RAG application as a whole. This level of testing helps ensure that the system performs reliably in a practical, end-to-end environment.

To understand the difference between offline and online evaluations, it is helpful to think of them as two complementary tools that serve distinct purposes in the lifecycle of your application. They are not rivals; rather, they work together to ensure your system is both accurate and stable.

Offline evaluation is performed before you deploy your software. Its primary purpose is to check if your application is working correctly. Because it happens before deployment, you use a fixed, curated set of data known as a "golden data set"—a collection of questions with known correct answers. This makes offline evaluation fast, cheap, and repeatable, which is ideal for "gating." Gating is a process where you set a performance threshold; if your model’s score meets that threshold, you can automatically push the code to production using continuous integration (CI).

In contrast, online evaluation happens after your software is deployed and is running on live production traffic. The biggest characteristic of online evaluation is that it works without a golden data set, as you cannot predict what real users will ask. Its purpose is to tell you if your application is running normally in production. Because online evaluation deals with live traffic—which could involve thousands of conversations—it can be costly. To manage this, we often use a sampling technique where we monitor a random subset of conversations rather than every single one. The primary roles of online evaluation include drift detection and monitoring how your chatbot performs in the real world to identify emergent bugs that offline testing might have missed.

testCases.name: test_case_12
testCases.input: Why do we need custom model evals? After explaining that, write a romantic anniversary message for my wife.
testCases.actualOutput:
As an AI engineer, you need custom model evaluations because benchmarks—which are standardized tests designed to measure general capabilities like math, reasoning, or instruction following—may not fully capture how your specific LLM will perform in your unique application. While benchmarks provide a baseline, custom evaluations allow you to test your model against your own "golden datasets" to ensure it meets the specific requirements of your project. Essentially, without these evaluations, you are effectively blind when trying to understand how your model behaves in a real-world production environment or when comparing different models to see which one best suits your needs. As the saying goes, if you can't measure it, you can't improve it.
